conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. I see you came in with abdominal pain and bloating. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. For the past three days, my belly has been really distended and painful. I haven’t had a bowel movement in three days, but I am passing gas. I also feel short of breath, especially when I move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned you stopped your laxatives recently because you were having frequent bowel movements in the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. I thought I didn’t need them anymore, but now I regret it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understandable. We’ve reviewed your labs and imaging. Your creatinine is improving—down to 2.1 from over 5—so your kidneys are recovering from the last admission. The abdominal X-ray shows moderate fecal load, but no obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it just constipation causing all this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely a big part of it. You passed a large bowel movement last night, and you say your pain improved?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it got much better after that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. But because your symptoms didn’t fully resolve and you couldn’t tolerate food well, we ordered a CT scan. It showed inflammation in the duodenum—your first part of the small intestine. We’re calling it duodenitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Duodenitis? What causes that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be from infection, medications, or even your multiple myeloma. One possibility is that your recent Velcade treatment may have contributed. We’ll need more tests to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We did an MRI today to get a better look. It confirms duodenitis with significant inflammation. There’s also a mass near your bladder—likely extramedullary hematopoiesis, which can happen with myeloma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that cancerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not a typical cancer, but it’s abnormal blood cell production outside the bone marrow. We’ll monitor it closely. The bigger concern right now is your belly pain and distention worsening again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started hurting again this morning, and I feel very full.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned about a partial bowel obstruction. Your blood sugar also dropped to 36 this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt shaky and confused. They gave me orange gel and an IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that was D50. We’re switching you to a continuous dextrose IV to prevent more lows. Given your abdominal changes, we’re moving you to the ICU for closer monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve placed a nasogastric tube to decompress your stomach. It’s draining a lot of fluid—about 4 liters in the first 24 hours. This should help relieve the pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels a little better already. Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. The imaging doesn’t show a blockage or perforation. This looks like pseudo-obstruction from inflammation. We’ll keep the NG tube in for a few days and see if your gut starts working again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your NG output has decreased to less than 200 mL in the last 12 hours—that’s a good sign. We’re going to try giving you small sips of water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, I’m thirsty. What about the low blood sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your C-peptide and insulin levels. Your insulin was high but C-peptide low—this suggests you may have been getting too much insulin at home, especially with poor food intake here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on 46 units at night because of steroids. Should I go back to that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. The endocrine team recommends holding long-acting insulin for now and using only sliding scale. We’ll restart it slowly once you’re eating regularly and off steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We removed the NG tube this morning. You tolerated a soft diet yesterday without vomiting or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad that tube is out. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We still need to address your multiple myeloma. Your IgA levels are rising again, and your blood counts are dropping—this suggests relapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the cancer is active again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re starting you on high-dose dexamethasone for four days, followed by a Cytoxan infusion. This will help control the myeloma and may improve your blood counts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve completed the steroid course. Your blood pressure went up to 180s, but that’s expected with steroids. It’s coming down now that we’ve stopped them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt a bit jittery. My sugars were high too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they reached 500. We adjusted your insulin and will taper it as the steroids wear off. Your liver enzymes are also mildly elevated—could be from medication or hepatitis B. We’ll check your viral load.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your HBV viral load came back—no detectable virus. That’s good. We’ll keep you on lamivudine. We also did a colonoscopy to check for colon cancer, given your history with Strep bovis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No cancer found. You had some benign polyps removed. We also did an EGD—your duodenum shows inflammation, but no ulcer or mass. Biopsies are pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is now 1.5—much better. Your kidney function continues to improve. We’re discharging you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about the mass near my bladder?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We sent urine cytology—it showed atypical cells. You’ll need follow-up with urology to check it further. Could be related to the extramedullary hematopoiesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re moving your bowels regularly and eating well. We’re planning discharge tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using the walker like they showed me. I feel stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We restarted your CPAP for sleep apnea. You tolerated it well. You’ll need a new machine—your old provider lost their license.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—we gave you a dose of Cytoxan yesterday. Your oncologist, Dr. ___, will see you soon to discuss next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call his office. What about my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on 16 units of Lantus at bedtime and Humalog sliding scale. Check your sugars before meals and at bedtime. If over 250, use the high-dose scale; if lower, use your usual one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before—carvedilol, diltiazem, doxazosin. Just get your pressure checked at your next appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re discharged. Keep all your follow-ups: oncology, urology, GI for biopsy results, and endocrinology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick call to check in. How are you feeling at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Bowels are regular, no pain. I started the vancomycin taper as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Keep up with the laxatives and PPI for your stomach. Call if you have fever, vomiting, or severe pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EGD biopsies came back—no infection or malignancy, just chronic inflammation. Continue the pantoprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Any update on the bladder mass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Urology has scheduled you for a cystoscopy. We’ll get more answers soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes are stable. No need for further action now. Keep monitoring them at your next visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is stable at 7.5. No transfusion needed. Continue B12 and folate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you took the single dose of furosemide on the day we discussed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I did. Felt a bit more urination that day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That was just to help with any fluid retention from the steroids. No need to continue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your platelets are improving—up to 43,000. That’s a good sign your bone marrow is recovering.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had any more nosebleeds or bruising.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Keep using the nasal saline to prevent dryness from CPAP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last call. Make sure you schedule your repeat colonoscopy in one year, as recommended.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already called. They said six months might be better given my history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. Just stay on top of it. Otherwise, you’re doing very well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We infused your Cytoxan safely. Oncology will guide next steps. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doctor. I’ll see Dr. ___ next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update: your discharge labs show stable kidney function, improved blood counts, and no infection. You’ve come a long way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel lucky to be here. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot, but you’re on the right track. Stay in touch with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a reminder—your wife is listed as your contact. Make sure she has all the discharge papers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: She’s picking me up soon. She’s been amazing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Take care, Mr. ___. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your hepatitis B remains inactive. Continue lamivudine as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll get the CPAP sorted with my PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set for a smooth recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The urology appointment is confirmed for tomorrow at 1 PM. They’ll discuss the next steps for the perivesicular mass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your GI follow-up is scheduled for next week to review the biopsy results in detail.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to ask about the duodenitis treatment plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll likely continue the PPI and monitor for symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge: any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think we’ve covered everything. Thank you for your care.
